prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- A 13-year-old Minnesota boy who has cancer has resumed chemotherapy treatments and is not responding well, a family spokesman said Friday. Doctors say Daniel Hauser's lymphoma responded well to a first round of chemotherapy in February. Danny Hauser started a second round of chemotherapy treatment this week, Jim Navarro said in a statement on the family's Web site, dannyhauser.com. "The doctor changed the number of chemotherapy drugs in the protocol submitted to the court. Danny is not tolerating the drugs well and has been vomiting all day. He is understandably angry and depressed about being forced to go through the ravages of chemotherapy again." Daniel underwent his first round of chemotherapy in February, a month after he was diagnosed with Hodgkin's lymphoma. But his parents were concerned about the treatment's side effects, which typically include nausea, and decided to end the chemotherapy regimen and pursue holistic treatments instead. When Daniel's oncologist learned of the decision to reject standard treatment, which doctors say is associated with a cure rate of as high as 90 percent, he asked a court to intervene to ensure the teen got chemotherapy. Doctors say that, without it, the disease would likely prove fatal. But last week, before the court could act, Colleen Hauser packed up her son and flew with him to Southern California, from where they were planning to continue to Mexico to seek alternative alternative medical treatment. She said he would have run on his own had she not helped him flee. She changed her mind before crossing the border and returned this week with Daniel to Minnesota, where the family agreed to comply with whatever treatment the court ordered. A medical examination revealed that the boy's tumor had grown since he was diagnosed and the boy's doctor recommended he resume chemotherapy. After examining the boy on Monday, Dr. Michael Richards estimated the tumor's size at 5.3 inches by 5.1 inches by 6.3 inches, and said it was "protruding outside the chest wall." He said initiation this week of standard chemotherapy treatment was "imperative." Richards recommended at least another five cycles of chemotherapy followed by radiation, and added that the "goal will be to include alternative therapies in which the family is interested, as long as there is not data to suggest that a particular danger exists with any alternative medicine." District Court Judge John Rodenberg originally took custody of the boy away from his parents, but returned him to his family on the condition that they comply with the recommendations of the cancer specialist. Hodgkin's lymphoma is a cancer that affects the lymphatic system, which is part of the immune system. As the disease progresses, it compromises a body's ability to fight infection. CNN's Aaron Cooper contributed to this story.

## CNN-Style News Report: Legal Battle Over 13-Year-Old Daniel Hauser’s Cancer Treatment

**SLEEPY EYE, Minnesota —** A Minnesota family’s refusal to continue chemotherapy for their 13-year-old son has sparked a high-profile legal and medical dispute, raising difficult questions about parental rights, religious freedom, and a child’s right to lifesaving medical care.

At the center of the case is **Daniel Hauser**, a teenager diagnosed with **Hodgkin’s lymphoma**, a cancer of the lymphatic system that doctors say is highly treatable with conventional medicine. Physicians testified that Daniel’s chances of survival were extremely high if he received chemotherapy and radiation, but far lower if he relied only on alternative treatments.

### Doctors Say Chemotherapy Offers Strong Chance of Survival

Daniel was diagnosed with Hodgkin’s lymphoma earlier in 2009. According to medical testimony, he initially underwent one round of chemotherapy, which doctors said caused his tumor to shrink. But Daniel and his parents, **Colleen and Anthony Hauser**, later stopped the treatment.

Doctors warned that without continued chemotherapy, Daniel’s cancer could progress and become life-threatening. Medical experts told the court that with standard treatment, Daniel had an estimated **80% to 90% chance of survival**, while his chances could drop dramatically without it.

Physicians recommended that Daniel continue a conventional treatment plan, including chemotherapy and possibly radiation, depending on follow-up scans and the extent of the disease.

### Family Rejects Treatment, Cites Beliefs and Side Effects

The Hauser family said they objected to chemotherapy because of its harsh side effects and because of their religious and personal beliefs. The family said they preferred natural remedies, including vitamins, herbs, and other alternative therapies.

Daniel and his mother have identified with the **Nemenhah Band**, a religious group that incorporates Native American healing practices. The family argued that forcing Daniel to undergo chemotherapy would violate their beliefs and their right to make medical decisions.

Daniel himself told the court he did not want more chemotherapy. However, testimony indicated he had limited understanding of his illness and treatment options. A court-appointed attorney and medical experts raised concerns about whether he was capable of making an informed decision.

### Judge Rules Daniel Is Medically Neglected

A Minnesota judge ruled that Daniel’s parents had **medically neglected** him by refusing recommended cancer treatment.

The judge found that Daniel’s Hodgkin’s lymphoma required immediate medical attention and that the parents’ decision to reject chemotherapy placed his life at risk. The ruling ordered the family to obtain updated medical testing, including imaging to determine whether the cancer had spread or worsened.

The judge also ordered that Daniel be evaluated by an oncologist and that he receive chemotherapy if doctors determined it was medically necessary. The court warned that if the family refused to comply, Daniel could be placed in the custody of child protective services for the purpose of receiving treatment.

### Court Emphasizes Child’s Welfare Over Parental Choice

In the ruling, the judge acknowledged the importance of parental rights and religious freedom but said those rights do not allow parents to deny a child lifesaving care.

The court concluded that the state has a duty to intervene when a child’s life is endangered by a refusal of medical treatment. The judge also determined that Daniel was not mature enough to fully understand the consequences of refusing chemotherapy.

The decision reflected a long-standing legal principle: parents generally have broad authority to make decisions for their children, but that authority can be limited when a child faces serious harm or death.

### Family Initially Resists, Then Responds to Court Pressure

The case drew national attention after Daniel and his mother briefly disappeared, missing a court-ordered medical appointment. Authorities believed they may have left Minnesota to avoid chemotherapy.

After several days, the two returned. Colleen Hauser later indicated the family would cooperate with the court’s order and pursue medical evaluation and treatment.

The family’s attorney said the Hausers loved their son and were trying to do what they believed was best for him, not neglect him. Supporters of the family argued that parents should have the right to choose alternative medicine. Critics said the refusal of chemotherapy amounted to risking a child’s life despite a strong chance of cure.

### A Case With Broader Implications

Daniel Hauser’s case became a flashpoint in the national debate over medical freedom, parental rights, religious beliefs, and child protection.

For doctors, the issue was straightforward: Hodgkin’s lymphoma is one of the more treatable forms of cancer, and delaying chemotherapy could reduce Daniel’s chances of survival.

For the family, the dispute centered on the right to reject what they viewed as harmful treatment and pursue healing methods aligned with their beliefs.

For the court, the deciding factor was Daniel’s welfare.

The judge’s ruling made clear that when a child has a potentially curable cancer, and when doctors say conventional treatment is necessary to save his life, the state can step in — even over the objections of the parents and the child.
